claims.text: Maximum capacity is the highest output a business can produce in a given period using the resources it already holds - its premises, its equipment, its staff and the hours it works. The figure is not a fixed physical fact: it depends on the shift pattern assumed, on the time set aside for maintenance and for changeovers between products, and on the product mix being made.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capacity utilisation = (current output / maximum possible output) x 100, expressed as a percentage. Current output and maximum output must be measured in the same units of output over the same period. The formula rearranges: current output = capacity utilisation x maximum output, and maximum output = current output / capacity utilisation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Spare capacity, also called excess capacity, is maximum capacity minus current output. It is measured in units of output; the same gap expressed as a percentage of maximum capacity is 100% minus the capacity utilisation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capacity utilisation matters chiefly because fixed costs are spread across output. Fixed cost per unit = total fixed costs / output, so the same fixed total carried by more units gives a lower fixed cost per unit and, with variable cost per unit unmoved, a lower total cost per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capacity utilisation is output measured against the maximum output possible, and it is a percentage. Labour productivity is output per worker or per labour hour, and it is a quantity. A business that puts more people onto an idle line can raise its capacity utilisation while output per worker is no higher than before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A capacity utilisation figure does not say whether the output was sold, does not say anything about the quality of what was made, and does not say whether the capacity itself is the right size for the market. It is therefore read against the business's own earlier figures, against the level it planned for, or against a competitor measuring capacity on the same basis, rather than alone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When output falls below maximum capacity, the fixed costs of the period are divided between fewer units, so fixed cost per unit rises and total cost per unit rises with it. At the same selling price the profit earned on each unit is smaller, and if output falls far enough the business makes a loss.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Under-utilisation leaves resources the business is already paying for standing idle - equipment, floor space and the hours of permanent staff - so capital is tied up in assets that are not earning and cash is committed to capacity that is producing nothing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where under-utilisation persists, employees can see idle equipment and may expect short-time working or redundancies. Motivation tends to fall and the most employable staff, who are often the most skilled, are the likeliest to leave. The effect tends to be stronger where the business has made redundancies recently.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Spare capacity also buys a business things a business at its limit cannot have: room to accept an unexpected order without paying a premium to fill it, time to carry out maintenance and staff training without stopping production, and room to grow into rising demand without first buying equipment. A business in a growing or unpredictable market may therefore hold some spare capacity deliberately.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working at or very close to maximum capacity gives the lowest fixed cost per unit, but it removes slack. Equipment runs with less time available for servicing, so unplanned breakdowns become more likely; staff work longer hours, so errors, accidents and absence tend to rise; and quality checks are the easiest thing to shorten, so defects and reworking tend to increase.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business whose demand exceeds its capacity can turn work away, quote a longer delivery time, or buy the extra output through overtime, extra shifts or a subcontractor. Turning work away gives up the contribution those sales would have earned and may send the customer to a competitor who can deliver; buying the extra output raises the cost per unit of the extra units above the in-house cost at normal rates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost per unit therefore does not fall without limit as capacity utilisation rises. It falls while fixed costs are being spread across more units produced at normal cost, and it can turn back up once the business is buying output beyond the level its resources are designed for, because that output is bought with overtime premiums, hired equipment or a subcontractor's price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capacity utilisation is a ratio of output to maximum capacity, so it can be raised in two ways: by increasing the output the business produces and sells, which raises the numerator, or by reducing maximum capacity, which lowers the denominator.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demand-side methods of raising capacity utilisation include promotion, a price reduction, selling into new markets or new customer groups, adding products that sell when the existing ones do not, and producing to another business's specification or under its brand. Each raises utilisation only where the extra sales actually arrive and are worth more than what it cost to win them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A price reduction raises capacity utilisation only where the extra volume more than replaces the contribution given up on the units the business was already selling. The volume needed to stand still can be calculated by dividing the total contribution the business currently earns by the new contribution per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Producing for another business - to its specification or under its brand - fills idle capacity without the business having to build its own demand, but the work is usually accepted at a thinner margin than own-brand sales and it leaves the business dependent on a customer that may also be a competitor and that may place the work elsewhere when the arrangement is renewed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Rationalisation raises capacity utilisation by reducing maximum capacity - closing a site, selling or mothballing equipment, or cutting a shift - and it reduces fixed costs at the same time. It costs money when it is done, through redundancy payments, equipment sold below its book value and leases that may have to be bought out, and it is slow and expensive to reverse if demand recovers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Matching capacity to demand through temporary or seasonal staff and flexible shift patterns raises the utilisation of the capacity actually used without permanently removing the ability to produce more. Its limits are that temporary staff are usually less experienced than permanent staff, and that a business whose peak coincides with other employers' peaks is competing with them for the same people.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A higher capacity utilisation figure is worth having only where the extra output is sold. Producing into stock raises the measured percentage while tying up cash in inventory and carrying the risk that the goods go unsold, so the figure improves while the business's position does not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing is paying another business to carry out an activity that the business could perform itself, so that the work is bought as a service instead of being produced in-house - a component bought rather than machined, deliveries run by a courier, or cleaning, payroll, catering or IT support placed with an outside firm.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing is about who performs an activity; offshoring is about where it is performed. An activity can be outsourced to a supplier in the same town without leaving the country, and it can be offshored to another country while remaining inside the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing replaces the fixed cost of holding capacity - premises, equipment, supervision and permanent staff - with a price paid per unit of work used. That lowers the fixed-cost base, so the business covers its costs at a lower output, and it makes total costs fall when activity falls, which is worth most where demand is seasonal or uncertain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing reduces total cost only where the supplier's price is below the in-house cost that is genuinely avoidable - the spending that would actually stop. Where premises, an equipment lease or a supervisor's salary continue regardless, that cost is unavoidable over the period in question and the supplier's price is added to it rather than replacing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing is one of the ways a business handles a capacity problem in either direction: a business at its limit can place the overflow with a supplier and meet extra demand without committing to equipment that would stand idle if demand fell back, and a business carrying more capacity than it uses can stop paying for it. Capacity bought from a supplier can also usually be obtained faster than capacity that has to be built.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A supplier that performs one activity for many customers may run it at a scale, and with equipment and experience, that a single customer's volume would not justify, so the work may be done better or more cheaply than in-house. Whether that advantage exists is a question about the particular supplier rather than something outsourcing provides by itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing transfers the work but not the responsibility. The business's own customers still hold the business to account for a late or defective delivery, so it keeps the reputational consequences of failure while losing direct control over quality and timing and learning about problems later than it would in-house. A contract can specify standards and penalties, but a penalty recovers money rather than a customer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Once in-house capability is closed, restoring it is slow and expensive, so the business negotiates the renewal from a weaker position than it held at the start and the supplier may seek a higher price. The risk is larger where few suppliers can do the work and smaller where several can.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A supplier that makes a business's component or runs its process learns how that business works and may serve its competitors. Where the activity is one the business competes on - its design, its recipe, the service customers choose it for - outsourcing risks handing over what distinguishes the business, a risk that is far smaller for a supporting activity such as cleaning or payroll.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing an activity performed in-house normally means the employees who performed it are made redundant or moved to other work, which brings a cost at the time, possible disruption while it happens, and an effect on the confidence of the staff who continue. What the business is obliged to do for those employees - notice, consultation and payments - depends on the law of the country in which it operates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether outsourcing suits a business turns on five questions: whether the activity is core or supporting, how much of the in-house cost is genuinely avoidable, whether the required standard can be specified and checked, how many suppliers could do the work, and how stable demand is. Volatile demand favours buying capacity by the unit; steady high volume favours owning it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Outsourcing carries costs of its own that in-house production did not need in the same form: specifying the work, inspecting what arrives, moving goods, and settling disputes. Where the supplier is in another country, transport time and exposure to movements in the exchange rate, where the supplier prices in its own currency, belong in the comparison as well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
